question.difficultyReason: Strengthen by ruling out an alternative explanation (instrument insensitivity). Trap (D) sounds like it supports 'current theory' and might seem to strengthen; trap (E) offers a tangential fact about neutron-star origins.
question.stimulus: The supernova event of 1987 is interesting in that there is still no evidence of the neutron star that current theory says should have remained after a supernova of that size. This is in spite of the fact that many of the most sensitive instruments ever developed have searched for the tell-tale pulse of radiation that neutron stars emit. Thus, current theory is wrong in claiming that supernovas of a certain size always produce neutron stars.
question.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most supernova remnants that astronomers have detected have a neutron star nearby.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sensitive astronomical instruments have detected neutron stars much farther away than the location of the 1987 supernova.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The supernova of 1987 was the first that scientists were able to observe in progress.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several important features of the 1987 supernova are correctly predicted by the current theory.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some neutron stars are known to have come into existence by a cause other than a supernova explosion.

explanations.correct: The argument assumes that if a neutron star existed at the supernova site, our instruments would have detected it. Showing that our instruments have detected neutron stars much farther away than this site directly bolsters that assumption and so strengthens the no-neutron-star-must-exist conclusion.
explanations.A: Consistent with the theory being right most of the time — does not strengthen the claim that this particular case refutes the theory.
explanations.C: Irrelevant — observation history doesn't speak to whether a neutron star exists now.
explanations.D: Weakens, if anything — the theory has predictive track record here.
explanations.E: Tangential; the question is about this supernova producing a neutron star, not other origins.

source.notes: Verbatim from LSAC public LR sample page.

question.difficultyReason: EXCEPT format reverses the task: four answers strengthen, one doesn't. Requires careful reading. Tests the lawyer's chain: basic-adequate understanding > detailed precision → simple language.
question.stimulus: Lawyer: Juries are traditionally given their instructions in convoluted, legalistic language. The verbiage is intended to make the instructions more precise, but greater precision is of little use if most jurors have difficulty understanding the instructions. Since it is more important for jurors to have a basic but adequate understanding of their role than it is for the details of that role to be precisely specified, jury instructions should be formulated in simple, easily comprehensible language.
question.questionStem: Each of the following, if true, strengthens the lawyer's argument EXCEPT:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most jurors are less likely to understand instructions given in convoluted, legalistic language than instructions given in simple, easily comprehensible language.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most jurors do not have an adequate understanding of their role after being given jury instructions in convoluted, legalistic language.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Jury instructions formulated in simple, easily comprehensible language can adequately describe the role of the jurors.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The details of the role of the jurors cannot be specified with complete precision in simple, easily comprehensible language.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Jurors do not need to know the precise details of their role in order to have an adequate understanding of that role.

explanations.correct: D says simple language can't be perfectly precise — which is irrelevant to the lawyer's argument, and if anything concedes a cost of simple language without strengthening the case for it. So D does NOT strengthen.
explanations.A: Strengthens — confirms simple language improves comprehension.
explanations.B: Strengthens — confirms the current legalese fails.
explanations.C: Strengthens — confirms simple language is still adequate.
explanations.E: Strengthens — confirms the trade-off is acceptable.

source.notes: Verbatim from LSAC 2015 Large Print LSAT PDF, section I question 3. Answer key not published in PDF; (D) is the defensible correct answer per EXCEPT-strengthen analysis.
